status: complete — all five books; selective in the royal, battle, and imprecatory psalms; see coverage_note; awaiting second-pass review
note: The Psalter is indexed in its own five books (1-41, 42-72, 73-89, 90-106, 107-150), one entry per psalm except where a psalm divides at a clear seam. The Scriptural Appendix assigns one psalm to each chapter as its anchor, and every one of those assignments is carried as a prior; in Book I they are Psalms 1, 8, 15, 16, 19, 24, 27, 34, and 39; in Book II, 51 and 63; in Book III, 82 and 84; in Book IV, 90, 92, 100, and 103; in Book V, 112, 119 (four priors, carried in four stanza entries), 127, 128, 131, 133, 139, and 141. Every psalm the appendix's table names is carried. Psalm 119 is indexed by stanza, grouped where consecutive stanzas make one point.
genre_note: The Psalms are prayer, not instruction, and they are indexed as prayer. A psalm that brings grief or complaint honestly before God enacts Sacred Lament, and is marked exemplifies; PR08 is tagged where the lament is the psalm's centre, not wherever a complaint appears, so that the count reflects anchors rather than mentions. The imprecations — prayers for the confusion or destruction of enemies — are not softened and are not tagged as models: where they bear on a practice the index says so (35:1-28, 41:4-13), and otherwise they are read as what they are, the honest voicing of rage to God rather than its enactment against a neighbour, which the curriculum's own account of lament permits. Superscriptions are included in the verse text as the WEB numbers them and are not separately interpreted. Royal and battle psalms are indexed only where they anchor something beyond the king's victory. The enthronement psalms of Book IV (93, 96-99) are gathered into a single cluster, since they make one claim in five hymns.
prediction_note: The indexing order said Psalms would settle Sacred Lament permanently, and C09 with it. Across the five books PR08 is tagged on 23 psalms or stanzas, against thirty-two anchors in the whole of the rest of the index; Psalm 62:8 ('pour out your heart before him') prescribes the practice outright, Psalm 102's superscription defines it, and Psalm 88 shows it with no resolution at all. C09 is reached 14 times, with both of the appendix's C09 psalms (63, 84) carried as priors. Whether that settles either is for the reviewer; the drafter wrote the forecast. Unforecast: the Psalter also gives the index its clearest internal tension, at Psalm 119:136 and 119:158, where the same poet weeps over and then loathes the same people, and both are recorded.
coverage_note: Book I, unindexed: Psalm 21, a royal thanksgiving whose second half celebrates the destruction of the king's enemies' descendants, and the battle portion of Psalm 18 (18:37-50). Book II, unindexed: Psalm 45, a royal wedding song (whose 45:4 — the king riding 'on behalf of truth, humility, and righteousness' — comes close to the three pillars without being their source); Psalms 47 and 48, Zion and kingship hymns; Psalm 53, which repeats Psalm 14, and Psalm 70, which repeats 40:13-17; Psalm 54, a brief petition with nothing not anchored elsewhere; Psalms 58 and 59, imprecations against corrupt judges and besiegers, the first ending with the righteous washing their feet in the blood of the wicked, which the index will not tag as a model and has no other reason to tag; Psalm 60, a national oracle after defeat; Psalm 64, a complaint against conspirators; and the battle imagery of Psalm 68 outside 68:4-10. Book III, unindexed: Psalm 76, a victory hymn, and Psalm 83, a national imprecation against a coalition of enemies. Book V, unindexed: Psalm 108, a composite of 57 and 60; Psalm 109, the harshest imprecation in the Psalter, whose 109:4 — 'In return for my love, they are my adversaries; but I am in prayer' — is the one line in it the index would anchor and cannot without carrying the curses of 109:6-19 with it; Psalm 110, a royal oracle, the most-quoted psalm in the New Testament and a Christological text rather than a formation one; Psalms 124, 125, 129, 132, 135 (which repeats 115:4-8), 140, and 144, which add nothing not anchored elsewhere or end in imprecation; Psalm 149, which places a two-edged sword in the hands of the saints to bind the kings of the nations; and Psalm 137:7-9, the blessing on whoever dashes Babylon's infants against the rock. The last is the verse most often cited against the Psalter. The index does not soften it or allegorise it, and does not let it disappear: it is the cry of people whose own children were killed, preserved in scripture as what grief can become, and the entry at 137:1-6 stops before it so that no formation tag is asserted over it.

entries.pericope: Like a tree planted by the streams of water
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 1 to C01: choosing the Way of Life, the tree and its roots. Two ways, two outcomes — the tree that bears fruit 'in its season' and the chaff the wind drives away — and the difference lies in what a person delights in and returns to 'day and night.' The book of prayer opens with the Two Ways.

entries.pericope: Now therefore be wise, you kings
entries.connection: A royal psalm in which the rulers of the earth plot against God and are laughed at, then addressed directly: 'be wise, you kings. Be instructed, you judges of the earth. Serve Yahweh with fear.' C16's argument that authority answers to a higher authority, put to the kings themselves.

entries.pericope: I laid myself down and slept. I awakened; for Yahweh sustains me
entries.connection: Written, the superscription says, while fleeing his own son. The enemies are many and say 'there is no help for him in God' — and the psalmist sleeps. A quiet soul in the worst circumstances, C22's, and the lifted head of C19's hope.

entries.pericope: Search your own heart on your bed, and be still
entries.connection: An evening psalm: 'Stand in awe, and don't sin. Search your own heart on your bed, and be still,' and it ends lying down in peace. The Daily Anchors close each day with an honest review — replay the day, name one failure and the desire beneath it — and this is the oldest instruction to do it, given for the bedtime hour. The gladness 'more than when their grain and their new wine are increased' is C10's joy independent of circumstance. Paired with Psalm 5, its morning counterpart.

entries.pericope: In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly
entries.connection: The morning half of the pair that Psalm 4 began: 'Yahweh, in the morning you shall hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.' The Daily Anchors begin each morning with a spoken choice and a watch for the day ahead; this is the morning watch in prayer. C09's secret place kept at a fixed hour, and C28's day as the unit. The petitions against enemies in 5:10 are read under the genre note.

entries.pericope: Every night I flood my bed. I drench my couch with my tears
entries.connection: The first of the seven penitential psalms. Anguish in body and soul, the question 'how long?', tears every night — and then the turn: 'Yahweh has heard the voice of my weeping.' Sacred Lament in its exact form: grief brought whole, nothing tidied, hope not abandoned, resolution not demanded. C19's healing begins in the same place.

entries.pericope: He travails with iniquity. He has conceived mischief, and brought forth falsehood
entries.connection: The psalmist submits himself to the test before he asks for vindication: 'if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands… let the enemy pursue my soul.' C04's mirror held up first. The wicked man is then described in the language of pregnancy — travailing, conceiving, bringing forth — the same anatomy of a failure James 1:14-15 uses and C21 teaches, and his violence returns on his own head.

entries.pericope: What is man, that you think of him?
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 8 to C24: wonder before creation, and the Discipline of Unknowing. Looking at the moon and stars, the psalmist asks the question that has no answer from his side — 'what is man, that you think of him?' — and answers only that he is crowned with glory. Reality exceeding one's grasp of it, received as wonder rather than as a problem.

entries.pericope: A high tower for the oppressed… the needy shall not always be forgotten
entries.connection: Thanksgiving for justice done, with its beneficiaries named: the oppressed, the afflicted whose cry he 'doesn't forget,' the needy who 'shall not always be forgotten,' the poor whose hope will not perish. C16's why-the-vulnerable-specifically, praised as the character of God, and C10's gratitude.

entries.pericope: Why do you stand far off, Yahweh?
entries.connection: The psalm opens with a complaint against God — why do you stand far off, why do you hide? — and then describes the predator who hunts the helpless and 'says in his heart, God has forgotten… He will never see it.' C21's attention to what is said in the heart. The lament ends not in an answer but in a confidence: 'you do see trouble and grief.' Sacred Lament that accuses God of absence and keeps addressing him; C16's helpless and fatherless as its subject.

entries.pericope: If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?
entries.connection: Advised to flee like a bird, the psalmist refuses: the foundations may be shaking, but 'Yahweh is in his holy temple.' The steadiness of C22's quiet soul under a counsel of panic.

entries.pericope: They speak with flattering lips, and with a double heart
entries.connection: A world of lying, flattery, and a double heart — 'with our tongue we will prevail. Our lips are our own' — set against words of Yahweh 'refined… seven times.' C04's audit of speech and C08's test of words: the honest word is the refined one, and the double heart is its opposite.

entries.pericope: How long, Yahweh? Will you forget me forever?
entries.connection: Four times 'how long' — forgotten, hidden from, sorrowing daily, overcome — and then, without any change of circumstance recorded, 'But I trust in your loving kindness.' The shortest complete lament in the Psalter and the clearest model of the practice: the complaint is not withdrawn, and the trust is not postponed until it is answered.

entries.pericope: Yahweh looked down from heaven… to see if there were any who understood
entries.connection: 'The fool has said in his heart, There is no God.' The failure is placed in the heart, and God looks down to see if any understand. C07's claim that the obstacle to sight is the condition of the one looking. Psalm 53 repeats this psalm and is not separately indexed.

entries.pericope: He who keeps an oath even when it hurts
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 15 to C04 and the Moral Audit, and C04 quotes 15:1-3. Who may dwell with God is answered entirely in conduct, and the list maps onto the audit's areas: truth spoken in the heart, no slander, no evil to a friend, an oath kept when it costs, no usury, no bribe.

entries.pericope: In your presence is fullness of joy
entries.connection: C10 takes 16:8-11 as its witness: joy as the consequence of where one stands — 'I have set Yahweh always before me' — not something manufactured. 'Yahweh assigned my portion and my cup… The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places': contentment with an allotted portion, which is C18's.

entries.pericope: Men of the world, whose portion is in this life
entries.connection: The psalmist asks to be kept 'as the apple of your eye' and hidden 'under the shadow of your wings' — C09's sheltered place — and contrasts himself with those 'whose portion is in this life,' who store up for their children. 'As for me, I shall see your face… I shall be satisfied.' C18's other portion.

entries.pericope: He brought me forth also into a large place. He delivered me, because he delighted in me
entries.connection: The cords of death, the cry from distress, and a deliverance pictured as an earthquake: 'He drew me out of many waters.' The reason given is not the psalmist's merit but God's delight — 'because he delighted in me.' C19's door, opened from the far side. The battle passages of 18:37-50 are not indexed.

entries.pericope: With the merciful you will show yourself merciful
entries.connection: 'With the merciful you will show yourself merciful. With the perfect man, you will show yourself perfect… With the crooked you will show yourself shrewd.' The moral order of C01 as correspondence: what one is shapes what one meets. And the strength given is credited to an unexpected quality — 'your gentleness has made me great' — which is C27's mercy as the summit rather than the weakness.

entries.pericope: The heavens declare the glory of God… Forgive me from hidden errors
entries.connection: C07 takes 19:1-3 and 19:7-8 as its witness: the order of creation and of the law both enlighten the eyes. The psalm ends with a question no self-examination can fully answer — 'Who can discern his errors? Forgive me from hidden errors' — and a prayer that presumptuous sins not gain dominion. The limit of self-knowledge, admitted at the end of a psalm about seeing.

entries.pericope: Some trust in chariots, and some in horses
entries.connection: A prayer for the king before battle, turning on one contrast: 'Some trust in chariots, and some in horses, but we trust the name of Yahweh our God.' C18's freedom from what one would naturally rely on.

entries.pericope: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
entries.connection: The lament Christ prayed from the cross. It begins with God's absence stated as fact and the past faithfulness of God set against it — 'Our fathers trusted in you… But I am a worm' — and descends to bones out of joint and garments divided by lot. Then, abruptly, 'you have answered me,' and the psalm ends in the widest circle in the Psalter: 'All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to Yahweh,' the humble eating and satisfied. Sacred Lament at its deepest, and its outcome C27's widening rather than a private relief.

entries.pericope: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing
entries.connection: C19 opens under the heading 'The Shepherd,' and this is the shepherd's psalm: green pastures, still waters, a restored soul, a table set in the presence of enemies, and goodness following 'all the days of my life.' The valley of the shadow is walked through, not avoided. C22's quiet soul in its most familiar words.

entries.pericope: He who has clean hands and a pure heart
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 24 to C07: clean hands and a pure heart, the cleansing of the inner gaze. Who may stand in the holy place is answered with the outer and the inner together, and with a refusal: one 'who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood.'

entries.pericope: Don't remember the sins of my youth… He will teach the humble his way
entries.connection: An acrostic prayer of a man asking to be taught — show me, teach me, guide me — and to have his past forgotten: 'Don't remember the sins of my youth… Remember me according to your loving kindness.' C19's door and C25's way, learned step by step by those humble enough to be instructed.

entries.pericope: Examine me, Yahweh, and prove me. Try my heart and my mind
entries.connection: The psalmist invites examination — 'try my heart and my mind' — which is the posture C21 takes from Psalm 139. The confidence of his self-report is high, and the index records it as a prayer for testing rather than a model of self-assessment; Interior Diagnosis warns that a self-examination which finds nothing is the one most worth repeating.

entries.pericope: One thing I have asked of Yahweh… that I may dwell in the house of Yahweh
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 27 to C03 and C11: mercy without fear, and the one thing asked — to dwell. 'Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear?' opens C03's witness; 'one thing I have asked… to dwell in the house of Yahweh all the days of my life' is C11's. 'When my father and my mother forsake me, then Yahweh will take me up.' 'Wait for Yahweh.'

entries.pericope: Who speak peace with their neighbors, but mischief is in their hearts
entries.connection: The psalmist asks not to be counted with those 'who speak peace with their neighbors, but mischief is in their hearts' — the gap between outer speech and inner intent that C04's audit calls inconsistency.

entries.pericope: Yahweh's voice is on the waters
entries.connection: Seven times 'the voice of Yahweh' — on the waters, breaking cedars, shaking the wilderness, stripping forests — and in the temple 'everything says, Glory!' The storm as the landscape C24 asks the reader to stand in. It ends quietly: 'Yahweh will bless his people with peace.'

entries.pericope: Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning
entries.connection: A thanksgiving that remembers the lament: 'I said in my prosperity, I shall never be moved… when you hid your face, I was troubled. I cried to you.' Then 'you have turned my mourning into dancing.' Sacred Lament recalled from its far side, with its test passed — the sorrow moved through and ended in praise. 'His anger is but for a moment. His favor is for a lifetime' is C19's proportion, and the dancing is C10's.

entries.pericope: Into your hand I commend my spirit… My times are in your hand
entries.connection: Christ's last words from the cross in Luke are this psalm's: 'Into your hand I commend my spirit.' The psalmist is wasted with grief, forgotten 'like a dead man,' slandered — and entrusts himself: 'my times are in your hand.' C18's surrender of what cannot be held, and C22's shelter 'away from the strife of tongues.' 'I said in my haste, I am cut off' is recorded and answered.

entries.pericope: When I kept silence, my bones wasted away
entries.connection: 'When I kept silence, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long… I acknowledged my sin to you. I didn't hide my iniquity… and you forgave.' The cost of delay and the relief of naming, in sequence. The Failure Recovery Protocol says return at once, name it plainly, without ceremony; this psalm is the testimony of a man who waited and then did not. C19 pairs it with Psalm 51.

entries.pericope: A horse is a vain thing for safety
entries.connection: Creation by a word — 'he spoke, and it was done' — and a God who 'fashions all of their hearts.' Then the reliance that fails: 'There is no king saved by the multitude of an army… A horse is a vain thing for safety.' C24's wonder and C18's freedom from false securities.

entries.pericope: Seek peace, and pursue it
entries.connection: C15 takes 34:12-14 as its witness, and comments: 'Pursue is an active verb. You chase peace; it does not wander into your house on its own.' The command is set in a psalm of a poor man who cried and was heard, and of a God 'near to those who have a broken heart' — C19's.

entries.pericope: They reward me evil for good
entries.connection: The centre of this imprecatory psalm is what the psalmist did for his enemies before they turned on him: 'when they were sick, my clothing was sackcloth. I afflicted my soul with fasting… I behaved myself as though it had been my friend or my brother.' And they 'rejoiced' at his fall. Unreciprocated Care is bearing ingratitude from those one has helped. The settling question — does the recipient behave badly toward the helper, or merely fail to repay? — is answered plainly: they rewarded evil for good. The psalmist's bearing of it is to take it to God rather than repay it himself; the prayers for their confusion are read under the genre note. Medium for that reason.

entries.pericope: He flatters himself in his own eyes, too much to detect and hate his sin
entries.connection: The wicked 'flatters himself in his own eyes, too much to detect and hate his sin,' and 'plots iniquity on his bed' — the bed where Psalm 4 told the faithful to search their hearts. Interior Diagnosis warns that a proud man examining himself will find faults that are safely minor and miss the one organising his life; this is that failure, named. Against it, 'in your light shall we see light' — sight that comes from outside, which is C06's.

entries.pericope: Don't fret because of evildoers… Better is a little that the righteous has
entries.connection: An acrostic of counsel to someone eaten up by the prosperity of the wicked: don't fret, don't envy, 'cease from anger, and forsake wrath. Don't fret, it leads only to evildoing.' C22's healed heart, measured by fretting rather than by belief. 'Better is a little that the righteous has, than the abundance of many wicked' is C18's. The righteous man 'deals graciously, and lends' 'all day long' and 'gives generously' — giving as a settled habit, which is Habitual Almsgiving, tagged at medium because it is described rather than commanded.

entries.pericope: I, as a deaf man, don't hear… in whose mouth are no reproofs
entries.connection: A penitential lament — 'my iniquities have gone over my head' — in which illness, guilt, and abandonment by friends are all brought to God: 'Lord, all my desire is before you. My groaning is not hidden from you.' Sacred Lament with confession inside it ('I will declare my iniquity'). And toward those who 'speak mischievous things,' silence: 'as a deaf man… as a mute man… in whose mouth are no reproofs.' Absorbing the Blow is adding nothing to the fire, keeping silent before hostility; medium, because the hostility here is plotting rather than open anger.

entries.pericope: I will keep my mouth with a bridle… I am a stranger with you, a foreigner
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 39 to C18: the stranger and sojourner. 'I am a stranger with you, a foreigner, as all my fathers were'; 'you have made my days handbreadths.' It opens with a watch kept over the tongue — 'I will watch my ways, so that I don't sin with my tongue. I will keep my mouth with a bridle while the wicked is before me' — and records the heat rising inside while the mouth is held: 'my heart was hot within me.' Watchfulness, with the movement of the heart observed and not acted on, and then turned into prayer rather than speech.

entries.pericope: You have opened my ears… your law is within my heart
entries.connection: 'I waited patiently for Yahweh… He brought me up also out of a horrible pit, out of the miry clay.' C19's rescue. And the inward turn: sacrifice not desired, 'you have opened my ears,' 'your law is within my heart' — the outward rite read inwardly, which is C06's reading, and the opened ear its organ.

entries.pericope: Blessed is he who considers the poor
entries.connection: The verb is attention — to consider, to give thought to the poor — and the blessing is on the one who does it habitually. C16's why-the-vulnerable-specifically, and Habitual Almsgiving's beginning: noticing. Medium, because the psalm blesses the attention without prescribing the giving.

entries.pericope: My own familiar friend… has lifted up his heel against me… that I may repay them
entries.connection: Sick and slandered, the psalmist is betrayed by the friend 'who ate bread with me' — the verse Christ applies to Judas in John 13:18. And he asks for strength 'that I may repay them.' The index records the prayer as it stands: Non-Retaliation's absence, honestly voiced in prayer, by a man who had first blessed those who consider the poor. The curriculum's practice is the answer the Gospels give to this verse, not an endorsement of it.

entries.pericope: As the deer pants for the water brooks… Why are you in despair, my soul?
entries.connection: One poem in two psalms, held together by its refrain. Thirst for God — 'my soul thirsts for God, for the living God' — and tears as food 'day and night' while others ask 'Where is your God?' Three times the psalmist questions his own soul and commands it in the same breath: 'Why are you in despair, my soul?… Hope in God!' Sacred Lament that argues with itself rather than with God alone, and that holds memory of past joy and present desolation side by side. C09's longing as the engine of prayer, and C19's hope commanded into a despairing heart.

entries.pericope: Wake up! Why do you sleep, Lord?
entries.connection: A communal lament with a protest of innocence at its centre: 'All this has come on us, yet have we not forgotten you… Our heart has not turned back.' The suffering has no moral root the people can find, and they say so to God directly — 'Wake up! Why do you sleep, Lord?… Why do you hide your face?' Sacred Lament in its boldest form, and suffering that exceeds explanation, which is the ground C24 asks the reader to stand on without forcing an answer. Paul quotes 44:22 in Romans 8:36.

entries.pericope: Be still, and know that I am God
entries.connection: Refuge in the middle of upheaval — 'though the earth changes, though the mountains are shaken into the heart of the seas' — and a river that gladdens the city while everything around it roars. The command at the end is to stop: 'Be still, and know that I am God.' C22's quiet soul, commanded rather than achieved, and C24's knowing that comes by stillness rather than by mastery.

entries.pericope: They name their lands after themselves
entries.connection: A wisdom psalm addressed to rich and poor together. No one can ransom a brother from death; the rich leave their wealth to others; 'their inward thought is that their houses will endure forever… They name their lands after themselves.' 'When he dies he shall carry nothing away.' C18's detachment argued from the grave, and C02's wisdom: 'a man who has riches without understanding is like the animals that perish.'

entries.pericope: What right do you have to declare my statutes… You sit and speak against your brother
entries.connection: God has no need of bulls — 'every animal of the forest is mine' — and asks instead for the sacrifice of thanksgiving: the outward rite read for its inward meaning, which is C06's. Then the indictment of the man who recites the covenant and lives against it: he consents with thieves, frames deceit, 'sit[s] and speak[s] against your brother.' C04's hearer who is not a doer, confronted by the God he quotes.

entries.pericope: Create in me a clean heart, O God
entries.connection: C19 takes 51:1-3, 51:10, and 51:17 as its witness, and the Scriptural Appendix names David — 2 Samuel 11-12 with Psalm 51 — as the model for the Failure Recovery Protocol: a man who 'names it without excuse or explanation of circumstances and throws himself on mercy.' 'For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me.' Then the request that is more than forgiveness: 'Create in me a clean heart… Renew a right spirit within me' — the change of heart C26 promises. 'A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.'

entries.pericope: I am like a green olive tree in God's house
entries.connection: Against the man whose 'tongue plots destruction, like a sharp razor,' who loves lying more than truth and 'trusted in the abundance of his riches,' the psalmist sets himself as an olive tree rooted in God's house. C04's audit of the tongue and C18's misplaced trust, in one portrait.

entries.pericope: It was not an enemy who insulted me… but it was you, my companion
entries.connection: 'I am restless in my complaint, and moan.' The wish to escape — 'Oh that I had wings like a dove!' — and the wound named precisely: an enemy he could have endured, 'but it was you, a man like me, my companion, and my familiar friend… His mouth was smooth as butter, but his heart was war.' Sacred Lament over betrayal, prayed 'evening, morning, and at noon,' and ending in 'cast your burden on Yahweh.' C15's broken fellowship, and C18's burden handed over. The thrice-daily prayer of 55:17 is the Jewish rhythm the Didache later assigns to the Lord's Prayer; PR30 is defined by that prayer and is not tagged here.

entries.pericope: You put my tears into your bottle
entries.connection: 'When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you' — fear and trust in the same sentence, not in sequence. And a single image of what God does with grief: 'You number my wanderings. You put my tears into your bottle. Aren't they in your book?' Sorrow kept, not dismissed. C22's quiet held inside fear, and C19's God who keeps account of tears.

entries.pericope: In the shadow of your wings, I will take refuge, until disaster has passed
entries.connection: Written, the superscription says, in a cave while hunted. Refuge 'until disaster has passed,' and then a heart made steady enough to sing: 'My heart is steadfast, God, my heart is steadfast… I will wake up the dawn.' C09's sheltered place, and C22's steadiness found inside it.

entries.pericope: Lead me to the rock that is higher than I
entries.connection: 'From the end of the earth, I will call to you, when my heart is overwhelmed. Lead me to the rock that is higher than I.' A refuge above oneself, sought from the far edge. The psalm ends in the ordinary keeping of a promise — 'that I may fulfill my vows daily' — which is C13's faithfulness.

entries.pericope: Pour out your heart before him
entries.connection: The psalm of silence — 'my soul rests in God alone… My soul, wait in silence for God alone' — contains the plainest command to lament in the Psalter: 'Trust in him at all times, you people. Pour out your heart before him.' Sacred Lament prescribed, and prescribed together with trust rather than against it. 'If riches increase, don't set your heart on them' is C18's, and the waiting silence is C22's.

entries.pericope: My soul thirsts for you… in a dry and weary land, where there is no water
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 63 to C09: thirst in the dry land, entering the secret place. 'Your loving kindness is better than life'; 'when I remember you on my bed, and think about you in the night watches… My soul stays close to you.' The final verses against enemies are read under the genre note.

entries.pericope: You crown the year with your bounty
entries.connection: 'Sins overwhelmed me, but you atoned for our transgressions' — and then the year described as God's work from furrow to harvest: rain softening the ridges, the hills 'clothed with gladness,' the valleys shouting for joy. 'You call the morning's dawn and the evening with songs of joy.' C24's landscape of wonder and C10's gratitude, in a harvest hymn.

entries.pericope: We went through fire and through water, but you brought us to the place of abundance
entries.connection: Testing described as refining — 'you have refined us, as silver is refined… We went through fire and through water' — and arriving at abundance. C25's formation through trial, not around it. And one sentence on what blocks prayer: 'If I cherished sin in my heart, the Lord wouldn't have listened.' Not the sin's arrival but its cherishing, which is C20's distinction between a thought received and a thought hosted.

entries.pericope: Let all the peoples praise you
entries.connection: The priestly blessing — 'God be merciful to us, bless us, and cause his face to shine on us' — asked so that God's way 'may be known on earth, and your salvation among all nations.' Blessing received for the sake of the widest circle, which is C27's.

entries.pericope: A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows… God sets the lonely in families
entries.connection: In a long processional hymn, a few verses define God by those he takes in: 'A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows… God sets the lonely in families. He brings out the prisoners with singing… You, God, prepared your goodness for the poor.' C16's vulnerable, and C14's household as the place the lonely are set. The battle imagery of the rest of the psalm is not indexed.

entries.pericope: I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; for comforters, but I found none
entries.connection: 'Save me, God, for the waters have come up to my neck!' Hated without cause, made 'a stranger to my brothers,' a byword for his very devotion — 'the zeal of your house consumes me' — mocked while he fasts, given vinegar for his thirst. 'I looked for some to take pity, but there was none.' The New Testament quotes it of the passion more than any psalm but 22. Sacred Lament that includes honest confession ('you know my foolishness') and the fiercest imprecations in Book II (69:22-28), which are read under the genre note. The alienation of the faithful from their own kin is C17's cost.

entries.pericope: Don't reject me in my old age… until I have declared your strength to the next generation
entries.connection: The prayer of an old man who has trusted God 'from the womb' and asks not to be abandoned 'when my strength fails' — and asks it for a reason: 'until I have declared your strength to the next generation.' He tells of God's righteousness 'though I don't know its full measure.' C25's long road walked to its end, and C14's handing on.

entries.pericope: He will deliver the needy when he cries; the poor, who has no helper
entries.connection: The prayer for the ideal king is a prayer that he will be measured by the poor: 'He will judge your people with righteousness, and your poor with justice… He will deliver the needy when he cries; the poor, who has no helper… Their blood will be precious in his sight.' C16's account of what authority is for, sung over a coronation.

entries.pericope: For I was envious of the arrogant… Until I entered God's sanctuary
entries.connection: The psalmist nearly falls, and traces the near-fall to its root in the third verse: 'For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.' He follows it through — the complaint that his own innocence was 'in vain,' the bitterness, 'I was so senseless and ignorant. I was a brute beast before you' — and names where the turn came: 'until I entered God's sanctuary, and considered their latter end.' Interior Diagnosis carried out in a single poem: the visible failure, the desire beneath it, the point where it was caught. The sanctuary that changes the sight is C09's secret place, and the resolution is a desire reordered — 'There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you.'

entries.pericope: We see no miraculous signs. There is no longer any prophet
entries.connection: A communal lament over the burned sanctuary: the enemy's axes in the carved work, the meeting places burned, 'no longer any prophet, neither is there among us anyone who knows how long.' The complaint is direct — 'Why do you draw back your hand?' — and is held against a recital of God's ancient power. Sacred Lament for a whole people, and its plea for the weakest: 'Don't forget the life of your poor forever… Let the poor and needy praise your name.'

entries.pericope: Neither from the east, nor from the west… comes exaltation
entries.connection: 'Don't boast… Don't lift up your horn on high.' Exaltation comes from no direction a person can travel; 'God is the judge. He puts down one, and lifts up another.' C16's warning to those who hold power, and C22's relational humility.

entries.pericope: Has God forgotten to be gracious?… Your footsteps were not known
entries.connection: 'My soul refused to be comforted.' The questions come in a sequence that has no softening — will he reject forever, has his loving kindness vanished, 'has God forgotten to be gracious?' — and then a decision: 'I will remember Yah's deeds.' Sacred Lament that does not resolve the question but turns toward memory. The psalm ends at the sea: 'Your way was through the sea; your paths through the great waters. Your footsteps were not known.' God's path is real and unrecoverable — the Discipline of Unknowing in an image, at medium because it is offered as praise rather than as a posture commanded.

entries.pericope: He, being merciful, forgave iniquity… He remembered that they were but flesh
entries.connection: A teaching psalm, told so that 'the generation to come might know, even the children who should be born; who should arise and tell their children' — C14's household as the carrier of memory. Its long history of rebellion is answered at the centre by mercy grounded in realism: 'they flattered him with their mouth… their heart was not right with him… But he, being merciful, forgave iniquity… He remembered that they were but flesh.' C19's door. It ends with David taken from the sheepfolds to shepherd 'according to the integrity of his heart' and 'the skillfulness of his hands,' which is C16's ruler.

entries.pericope: Don't hold the iniquities of our forefathers against us
entries.connection: Jerusalem in heaps and the dead unburied; 'How long, Yahweh?' The lament asks forgiveness for the people's own sins and those of their fathers, and asks for 'the sighing of the prisoner' to come before God. The prayer for sevenfold repayment of the neighbours (79:12) is read under the genre note.

entries.pericope: You brought a vine out of Egypt… Turn us again, God
entries.connection: Three times the refrain: 'Turn us again… cause your face to shine, and we will be saved.' At its centre the image C11 builds on: a vine brought out of Egypt and planted, filling the land, and now broken down and ravaged — 'visit this vine.' Christ's 'I am the true vine' answers this psalm and Isaiah 5. A people 'fed… with the bread of tears' bringing that grief to God is Sacred Lament.

entries.pericope: So I let them go after the stubbornness of their hearts
entries.connection: God speaks: 'Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it. But my people didn't listen… So I let them go after the stubbornness of their hearts, that they might walk in their own counsels.' The judgment is to be given what one has chosen. C21's account of a heart that becomes its own master, and C20's reason for attending to it early. 'Oh that my people would listen to me.'

entries.pericope: Defend the weak, the poor, and the fatherless
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 82 to C16, and C16 takes 82:1-4 as its witness: God in the assembly of the powerful, asking 'How long will you judge unjustly?' and commanding, 'Defend the weak, the poor, and the fatherless. Maintain the rights of the poor and oppressed.' Authority is judged by what it does for those with none.

entries.pericope: Passing through the valley of Weeping, they make it a place of springs. They go from strength to strength
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 84 to three chapters: the sparrow's nest (C09), the valley of Weeping and the day in your courts better than a thousand (C18), and strength to strength (C25), which C25 takes as its witness at 84:5. The pilgrim's road is walked by stages — 'they go from strength to strength' — and the valley of tears is not avoided but transformed by those passing through. The Discipline of Gradualism's picture of the life: not arrival, but the next stage of the road.

entries.pericope: Mercy and truth meet together. Righteousness and peace have kissed each other
entries.connection: After forgiveness and a plea for revival comes the curriculum's two pillars in a single line: 'Mercy and truth meet together. Righteousness and peace have kissed each other. Truth springs out of the earth. Righteousness has looked down from heaven.' C01's claim that truth without mercy turns harsh and mercy without truth turns sentimental, imaged as a meeting rather than a balance. The peace spoken 'to his people' is C15's.

entries.pericope: Make my heart undivided to fear your name
entries.connection: 'Teach me your way, Yahweh. I will walk in your truth. Make my heart undivided to fear your name.' C26 opens with 'The Divided Heart' and promises its healing; this is the prayer for it. And the character of the God addressed — 'merciful and gracious… slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth' — is the mature mercy of C27.

entries.pericope: I will record Rahab and Babylon among those who acknowledge me… This one was born there
entries.connection: God enrolls the nations as natives of Zion — Egypt (Rahab), Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, Ethiopia, the oppressors and enemies of Israel's history — and writes beside each: 'This one was born there.' The circle widened until even former enemies stand inside it, which is C27's, and the Scriptural Appendix grounds Shedding Harshness in exactly this movement at Isaiah 56. Medium: the widening is God's act, and the practice is the human disposition that imitates it.

entries.pericope: You have put lover and friend far from me, and my friends into darkness
entries.connection: The only psalm that never turns. Cried 'day and night,' laid 'in the lowest pit,' cut off from friends, 'afflicted and ready to die from my youth up' — and it ends in darkness, with no recovered confidence. Sacred Lament without demanding immediate resolution, preserved in scripture without one. The practice's own word of care belongs here: grief that has flattened everything for months may not be a spiritual matter at all, and should be brought to someone competent as well as to God. The psalm's presence in the canon is the assurance that such prayer is not failed prayer.

entries.pericope: Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne. Loving kindness and truth go before your face
entries.connection: A hymn to the faithfulness of God and his covenant with David, with the moral order described as the architecture of the throne: 'Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne. Loving kindness and truth go before your face.' C01's grain of reality, and its pillars, set at the base of everything.

entries.pericope: But you have rejected and spurned… Remember how short my time is!
entries.connection: Then the turn, without warning: 'But you have rejected and spurned.' The covenant just praised appears broken, and the psalmist says so — 'Lord, where are your former loving kindnesses, which you swore to David?' Sacred Lament that holds God to his own words. 'Remember how short my time is!' is C28's numbering of days, prayed in protest rather than resignation. Book III ends with a doxology that follows the complaint without cancelling it.

entries.pericope: So teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 90 to C28: numbering our days, the day as the unit of formation, and C28 takes 90:12 as its witness. A thousand years 'like yesterday when it is past,' a life of seventy or eighty years that 'passes quickly, and we fly away' — and the request that follows is not for more time but for wisdom about the time there is. It ends asking God to 'establish the work of our hands,' the ordinary labour of a single day made lasting.

entries.pericope: He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High
entries.connection: 'He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High will rest in the shadow of the Almighty.' C09 is named for this place. The promises that follow are the psalm the tempter quotes to Christ in Matthew 4, which is a reminder that they describe trust, not a guarantee to be tested.

entries.pericope: They will still bring forth fruit in old age
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 92 to C23: the cedar, hidden growth, and fruit in old age, which C23 takes as its witness at 92:12-14. The righteous 'planted in Yahweh's house… will still bring forth fruit in old age. They will be full of sap and green.' The song for the Sabbath also sets the shape of a day: 'to proclaim your loving kindness in the morning, and your faithfulness every night' — the Daily Anchors' morning and evening, given to praise. PR07 at medium for that reason; the prior is C23's.

entries.pericope: In the multitude of my thoughts within me, your comforts delight my soul
entries.connection: 'They kill the widow and the alien, and murder the fatherless. They say, Yah will not see.' The answer to the oppressors is a question — 'He who formed the eye, won't he see?' — and the answer to the psalmist's own anxiety is a confession: 'When I said, My foot is slipping! Your loving kindness, Yahweh, held me up. In the multitude of my thoughts within me, your comforts delight my soul.' C16's vulnerable defended, and C22's quieting of an anxious mind.

entries.pericope: Today, oh that you would hear his voice! Don't harden your heart
entries.connection: A call to worship that turns into a warning: 'Today, oh that you would hear his voice! Don't harden your heart, as at Meribah.' The appeal is always for today — Hebrews 3-4 builds an argument on the word — which is C28's unit, and the danger is a heart that hardens by degrees, which is what C20 watches for. 'It is a people that errs in their heart.'

entries.pericope: The enthronement psalms
entries.connection: Five hymns of God's kingship gathered as one theme: the floods lifting their voice and Yahweh mightier than the breakers (93); a new song for all the earth, the trees of the forest singing (96); clouds and darkness around a throne founded on righteousness and justice (97); the rivers clapping their hands (98); and the holy God who 'forgave them, although you took vengeance for their doings' (99). C24's wonder is their whole register, and their scope is C27's: the nations, the islands, 'all the earth' summoned to the same joy.

entries.pericope: Enter into his gates with thanksgiving
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 100 to C10: gratitude and thanksgiving. 'Serve Yahweh with gladness… It is he who has made us, and we are his… Enter into his gates with thanksgiving.' C10's discipline of gratitude, grounded in belonging rather than in circumstance.

entries.pericope: I will walk within my house with a blameless heart
entries.connection: A ruler's vow, and it begins at home: 'I will walk within my house with a blameless heart. I will set no vile thing before my eyes.' C14's practice is to measure the difference between how one speaks inside the home and outside it; this vow makes the house the first place integrity is kept. What is allowed before the eyes is C07's. The closing resolve to destroy the wicked 'morning by morning' is a king's and is not what the entry anchors.

entries.pericope: A Prayer of the afflicted, when he is overwhelmed and pours out his complaint before Yahweh
entries.connection: The superscription is a definition of Sacred Lament: the prayer of the afflicted, overwhelmed, pouring out his complaint before Yahweh. Days consumed like smoke, a heart withered like grass, 'I forget to eat my bread… like a sparrow that is alone on the housetop… I have eaten ashes like bread, and mixed my drink with tears.' Then, without retracting any of it, the turn to the one who remains: 'They will perish, but you will endure… you will change them like a cloak.' C19's hope, and C18's recognition that everything else wears out.

entries.pericope: He remembers that we are dust
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 103 to C29 — 'He remembers that we are dust — the closing word of the book' — and C29 takes 103:8 as its final witness. 'He will not always accuse; neither will he stay angry forever. He has not dealt with us according to our sins… As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.' Merciful Reintegration is receiving the repentant back without lingering shame or permanent probation; this is God's own practice of it, described as a father's compassion, and the reason the curriculum ends here. PR29 at medium, because the reintegration is God's, and the practice is its human imitation.

entries.pericope: Man goes forth to his work, to his labor until the evening
entries.connection: Creation sung in its detail — springs in the valleys, the stork in the fir trees, the young lions seeking their food from God, leviathan 'formed to play' in the sea. Into this ordered world 'man goes forth to his work, to his labor until the evening,' and wine, oil, and bread are given 'that strengthens man's heart.' C24's landscape of wonder, with ordinary human work set inside it at its proper size, which is C28's.

entries.pericope: Until the time that his word happened
entries.connection: Israel's history retold as God's faithfulness: 'when they were but a few men in number… and foreigners in it. They went about from nation to nation.' Joseph's feet bruised in shackles 'until the time that his word happened.' C17's sojourners, and C25's promises kept on a schedule longer than any one life.

entries.pericope: He gave them their request, but sent leanness into their soul
entries.connection: A confession that begins in the present tense — 'We have sinned with our fathers' — and retells the wilderness as a history of forgetting. One verse names a judgment that operates from within: 'He gave them their request, but sent leanness into their soul.' Getting what one craves and being emptied by it is C21's diagnosis. Moses 'stood before him in the breach,' and the ending is C19's: 'Nevertheless he regarded their distress, when he heard their cry.' The psalm's complaint that the people did not destroy the nations (106:34) is part of the confession's argument and is not what the entry anchors.

entries.pericope: Then they cried to Yahweh in their trouble, and he delivered them
entries.connection: Four portraits of distress — wanderers with no city, prisoners in iron 'because they rebelled,' fools sick from their own iniquity, sailors at their wits' end — and four times the same sentence: 'Then they cried to Yahweh in their trouble, and he delivered them.' Some of the trouble is self-inflicted and the door opens anyway, which is C19's. 'Whoever is wise will pay attention to these things' is C02's.

entries.pericope: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom
entries.connection: An acrostic hymn whose last line is the entrance requirement C02 takes from Proverbs 1:7: 'The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom.' God's works are 'pondered by all those who delight in them' — study as delight, which is C24's.

entries.pericope: Light dawns in the darkness for the upright… He has dispersed, he has given to the poor
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 112 to C14, and C14 takes 112:4 as its witness for the harder seasons: 'Light dawns in the darkness for the upright, gracious, merciful, and righteous' — within the darkness, not instead of it. The portrait of the upright man is a portrait of habitual generosity: he 'deals graciously and lends,' and 'he has dispersed, he has given to the poor' — the verse Paul quotes in 2 Corinthians 9:9 of the collection for Jerusalem. Habitual Almsgiving as the shape of a household.

entries.pericope: He raises up the poor out of the dust… that he may set him with princes
entries.connection: The God enthroned on high 'stoops down to see,' and what he sees is the poor in the dust and the needy on the ash heap, whom he sets with princes, and the barren woman, whom he settles as a joyful mother. C16's why-the-vulnerable-specifically, as the character of God. PR25 is not tagged: the reversal is God's, and the practice is giving up one's own seat in a gathering, the distinction that has drawn PR25 in error before.

entries.pericope: Not to us, Yahweh, not to us… Those who make them will be like them
entries.connection: 'Not to us, Yahweh, not to us, but to your name give glory' — the refusal of credit that is the hidden life's, C23's. Then the idols: mouths that do not speak, eyes that do not see — 'Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.' C26's mechanism stated in reverse: we are transformed into what we behold, and those who behold what cannot see become unseeing. Psalm 135:15-18 repeats the passage and is not separately indexed.

entries.pericope: Return to your rest, my soul… What will I give to Yahweh for all his benefits?
entries.connection: Rescued from 'the cords of death,' the psalmist speaks to his own soul — 'Return to your rest, my soul' — and records an honest lapse: 'I said in my haste, All men are liars.' Then the question that gratitude asks: 'What will I give to Yahweh for all his benefits toward me?' C22's quieted soul, and C10's thanksgiving, paid as vows 'in the presence of all his people.'

entries.pericope: Praise Yahweh, all you nations!
entries.connection: The shortest psalm, and its scope is the widest: 'Praise Yahweh, all you nations! Extol him, all you peoples!' C27's circle, in two verses.

entries.pericope: This is the day that Yahweh has made. We will rejoice and be glad in it!
entries.connection: 'It is better to take refuge in Yahweh, than to put confidence in man… than to put confidence in princes' — C18's misplaced trust named twice. 'Yah has punished me severely, but he has not given me over to death.' And the line that makes a single day the unit of joy: 'This is the day that Yahweh has made. We will rejoice and be glad in it!' C28's day, received rather than managed. The rejected stone become the cornerstone (118:22) is quoted of Christ in all three Synoptics and in 1 Peter 2.

entries.pericope: Blessed are those whose ways are blameless, who walk according to Yahweh's law
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns 119:1-2 to C12: walking in truth. The longest psalm opens with a blessing on those who walk in the law and 'seek him with their whole heart,' and then a confession of the gap: 'Oh that my ways were steadfast to obey your statutes!' The walk is the proof, and the psalmist knows he has not yet walked it.

entries.pericope: I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you
entries.connection: 'How can a young man keep his way pure? By living according to your word… I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.' The guard is set before the temptation arrives, by what has been stored inside — the forward provision C20 makes against the movements it watches for.

entries.pericope: Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law. I am a stranger on the earth
entries.connection: Two priors in two consecutive verses. The Scriptural Appendix assigns 119:18 to C06 — 'Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law,' the prayer of the whole second stage — and 119:19 to C17 — 'I am a stranger on the earth. Don't hide your commandments from me,' which C17 takes as its witness. Sight asked for rather than assumed, by someone who knows he is not at home. 'Though princes sit and slander me, your servant will meditate on your statutes.'

entries.pericope: I run in the path of your commandments, for you have set my heart free
entries.connection: 'My soul is laid low in the dust… My soul is weary with sorrow.' Then an account given — 'I declared my ways, and you answered me' — and a change in the experience of obedience: 'I run in the path of your commandments, for you have set my heart free.' C19's revival from the dust, and C10's movement from duty to delight: the same path, run instead of trudged.

entries.pericope: Turn my heart toward your statutes, not toward selfish gain. Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things
entries.connection: Two turnings asked for, of the heart and of the eyes: 'Turn my heart toward your statutes, not toward selfish gain. Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things.' C07's cleansing of the lens and C18's release from gain, both requested rather than achieved — the psalmist does not trust himself to make the turn unaided.

entries.pericope: Your statutes have been my songs, in the house where I live
entries.connection: Two stanzas of a man under mockery who will 'speak of your statutes before kings' and 'walk in liberty.' 'This is my comfort in my affliction… Your statutes have been my songs, in the house where I live' — the house of his sojourning, the same word as 119:19's stranger. 'I have remembered your name, Yahweh, in the night.' C17's citizen-stranger singing in a borrowed house, and C09's night prayer.

entries.pericope: I considered my ways, and turned my steps to your statutes. I will hurry, and not delay
entries.connection: 'Yahweh is my portion' — C18's. And the shortest description of repentance in the Psalter: 'I considered my ways, and turned my steps to your statutes. I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.' The Failure Recovery Protocol says return the same day, at the next available moment, with no ceremony; this is that rule, kept by a man who examined his ways and did not wait. 'At midnight I will rise to give thanks to you.'

entries.pericope: It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn your statutes
entries.connection: 'Before I was afflicted, I went astray; but now I observe your word… It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn your statutes… In faithfulness you have afflicted me.' Affliction read, after the fact, as formation — C25's long road, on which the hard stretches are part of the way rather than detours from it. The comfort asked for in 119:76 is C19's. The index does not read these verses as a claim that all suffering is sent for instruction; the psalmist says it of his own.

entries.pericope: I have become like a wineskin in the smoke… When will you comfort me?
entries.connection: 'My soul faints for your salvation… My eyes fail for your word. I say, When will you comfort me? For I have become like a wineskin in the smoke' — dried out, blackened, cracking. 'How many are the days of your servant?' The lament stanza of the long psalm, and its refusal: 'They had almost wiped me from the earth, but I didn't forsake your precepts.'

entries.pericope: I have seen a limit to all perfection, but your commands are boundless
entries.connection: The word settled in heaven, a faithfulness 'to all generations,' and one line on the limits of everything else: 'I have seen a limit to all perfection, but your commands are boundless.' C24's measure — every human achievement has an edge, and what the psalmist loves has none. 'Unless your law had been my delight, I would have perished in my affliction' is C10's.

entries.pericope: Through your precepts, I get understanding; therefore I hate every false way
entries.connection: 'How I love your law! It is my meditation all day.' Wisdom beyond his enemies, his teachers, and the aged, because of what he keeps rather than what he knows — C02's skill of living. The Scriptural Appendix assigns 119:104-105 to C08, 'understanding before discernment': 'Through your precepts, I get understanding; therefore I hate every false way.' Discernment as the fruit of obedience, not its precondition.

entries.pericope: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path
entries.connection: C08 takes 119:105 as the companion of its whole chapter: 'Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.' A lamp for the next step, not a floodlight for the whole road. 'My soul is continually in my hand, yet I won't forget your law' — the danger is real, and the lamp is carried through it.

entries.pericope: I hate double-minded men… You are my hiding place and my shield
entries.connection: 'I hate double-minded men, but I love your law.' The divided heart that C26 opens with, rejected first in others and then implicitly in himself. 'You are my hiding place and my shield' is C09's sheltered place. 'My flesh trembles for fear of you.'

entries.pericope: Streams of tears run down my eyes, because they don't observe your law
entries.connection: 'The entrance of your words gives light. It gives understanding to the simple' — light given to those with least claim to it, which is C06's sight. And the stanza ends with grief rather than indignation at others' failure: 'Streams of tears run down my eyes, because they don't observe your law.' Shedding Harshness measures the mature heart by the movement it feels at another's downfall; here the movement is tears. Medium, because the same psalm records the opposite movement at 119:158, and the index records both.

entries.pericope: I am small and despised. I don't forget your precepts
entries.connection: 'My zeal wears me out… I am small and despised. I don't forget your precepts.' Faithfulness from someone who counts for nothing in the eyes of others and keeps going — C23's hidden life in a single line.

entries.pericope: I rise before dawn and cry for help… My eyes stay open through the night watches
entries.connection: 'I rise before dawn and cry for help. I put my hope in your words. My eyes stay open through the night watches, that I might meditate on your word.' Prayer fixed at the edges of the day and the hours of the night, which is C28's rhythm and C09's place. Together with 119:62 (midnight) and 119:164 (seven times a day), these verses are the scriptural root of the monastic hours; PR30's fixed-hour devotion is defined by the Lord's Prayer and is not tagged here.

entries.pericope: I look at the faithless with loathing, because they don't observe your word
entries.connection: Twenty-two verses after weeping over those who do not keep the law (119:136), the psalmist says: 'I look at the faithless with loathing, because they don't observe your word.' The same failure in others, met first with tears and then with loathing. Shedding Harshness is the slow widening of the circle until no one stands outside it; this verse is the circle drawn tight again, recorded honestly in the most devoted poem in scripture. The index keeps both entries so that the psalm's own unevenness is visible.

entries.pericope: Seven times a day, I praise you… Those who love your law have great peace
entries.connection: 'Seven times a day, I praise you, because of your righteous ordinances. Those who love your law have great peace. Nothing causes them to stumble.' Praise by the clock, which is C28's rhythm, and a peace that keeps the feet, which is C22's. 'All my ways are before you' — a life lived without a hidden compartment.

entries.pericope: I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant
entries.connection: After a hundred and seventy-five verses of love for the law, the psalm ends not with a claim of faithfulness but with a confession: 'I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant, for I don't forget your commandments.' The most devoted voice in the Psalter closes as a sheep needing to be found. C19's shepherd, and the parable of Luke 15 in a single verse.

entries.pericope: I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war
entries.connection: The first Song of Ascents begins in exile among the tents of Kedar, 'too long with him who hates peace. I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war.' C17's stranger in a hostile land, and C15's peace pursued even where the other party refuses it.

entries.pericope: He who keeps you will not slumber
entries.connection: 'I will lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from?' Six times the verb keep: a keeper who neither slumbers nor sleeps, who keeps 'your going out and your coming in.' C22's quiet soul resting on a vigilance not its own.

entries.pericope: For my brothers' and companions' sakes, I will now say, Peace be within you
entries.connection: 'Pray for the peace of Jerusalem.' The pilgrim asks peace for the city 'for my brothers' and companions' sakes… I will seek your good.' C15's peace as a thing sought for others, and C13's community as its occasion.

entries.pericope: As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master
entries.connection: Attention as prayer: 'as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master… so our eyes look to Yahweh, our God, until he has mercy on us.' The people are filled with 'the contempt of the proud' and answer it with watchful dependence. C22's relational humility, turned upward.

entries.pericope: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy
entries.connection: 'He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.' The weeping and the sowing happen together, and the harvest comes later. C25's long view, in which work done in grief is not wasted, and C19's restored fortunes 'like the streams in the Negev.'

entries.pericope: Unless Yahweh builds the house, they labor in vain who build it
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 127 to C26: unless Yahweh builds the house. The temple of light is not self-constructed. 'It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil; for he gives sleep to his loved ones' — C18's freedom from the anxious labour that thinks everything depends on it.

entries.pericope: Your children like olive plants, around your table
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 128 to C14, and C14 takes 128:1-2 as its witness: a quiet domestic psalm — honest work, a table, children around it, the household in order. 'You will eat the labor of your hands. You will be happy.'

entries.pericope: If you, Yah, kept a record of sins, Lord, who could stand? But there is forgiveness with you
entries.connection: 'Out of the depths I have cried to you.' The penitential psalm turns on a question that has no answer from the human side — 'If you, Yah, kept a record of sins, who could stand?' — and an answer from God's: 'But there is forgiveness with you.' Then waiting, 'more than watchmen long for the morning.' Sacred Lament from the depths, and C19's door at its most compact.

entries.pericope: Nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 131 to C22, and C22 takes 131:1-2 as its witness: the weaned child, the quiet soul. 'My heart isn't haughty, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me. Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul.' The first verse is also the Discipline of Unknowing in its plainest form: the disciplined recognition that some things exceed one's grasp, and the peace of not reaching for them.

entries.pericope: See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 133 to three chapters — C12, C13, and C15 — under 'oil and dew descending; unity in shared life,' and C12 and C13 take it as their witness. Unity pictured as something that runs down from above: oil from the head to the beard to the hem, dew from Hermon to the hills of Zion. 'For there Yahweh gives the blessing.'

entries.pericope: All you servants of Yahweh, who stand by night in Yahweh's house
entries.connection: The last Song of Ascents is addressed to those who keep the night watch in the temple: 'Lift up your hands in the sanctuary.' Prayer kept through the night by those whose service is unseen — C09's place and C28's hours.

entries.pericope: For his loving kindness endures forever
entries.connection: Twenty-six lines, each answered by the same refrain. Creation, exodus, wilderness, and then the line closest to the worshipper: 'Who remembered us in our low estate… Who gives food to every creature.' Gratitude formed by repetition rather than novelty, which is C10's discipline practised in C28's way.

entries.pericope: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down. Yes, we wept
entries.connection: Exiles weep by foreign rivers and hang up their harps when their captors demand 'one of the songs of Zion.' 'How can we sing Yahweh's song in a foreign land?' Sacred Lament for a lost home, and C17's question at its most painful: how to remain anchored elsewhere while living, against one's will, here. The entry stops at 137:6. The psalm ends (137:7-9) with a blessing on whoever dashes Babylon's infants against the rock; see the coverage note.

entries.pericope: Though Yahweh is high, yet he looks after the lowly
entries.connection: 'Though Yahweh is high, yet he looks after the lowly; but the proud, he knows from afar.' The distance God keeps is from pride, not from lowliness — C22's humility and C16's lowly as those God draws near. 'Yahweh will fulfill that which concerns me.'

entries.pericope: Search me, God, and know my heart… This knowledge is beyond me
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 139 to C21: 'Search me — the invited examination.' C21 takes 139:1-2 and 139:23-24 as its witness. The psalm begins with being known completely — 'you perceive my thoughts from afar… there is not a word on my tongue, but… you know it' — and ends asking for it: 'Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me.' Interior Diagnosis in its humble form, the examination handed to someone who can see what the self cannot. And at its centre, the Discipline of Unknowing: 'This knowledge is beyond me. It's lofty. I can't attain it.' The 'perfect hatred' of 139:19-22 sits immediately before the request to be searched, and the index reads the request as the psalm's own answer to it.

entries.pericope: Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix assigns Psalm 141 to C04 and C20, 'guarding the mouth and the gate of the heart,' and C20 takes 141:3 as its witness: 'Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips. Don't incline my heart to any evil thing.' Watchfulness asked for as a gift. And a second discipline beside it: 'Let the righteous strike me, it is kindness; let him reprove me, it is like oil on the head; don't let my head refuse it' — correction received as mercy, which is where C04's audit becomes bearable.

entries.pericope: I pour out my complaint before him. I tell him my troubles
entries.connection: Written, the superscription says, in the cave. 'I pour out my complaint before him. I tell him my troubles… there is no one who is concerned for me. Refuge has fled from me. No one cares for my soul.' Sacred Lament described by the one doing it. Then: 'You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living' — C18's portion, claimed with nothing else left.

entries.pericope: Don't enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no man living is righteous
entries.connection: The last penitential psalm asks for mercy on the only ground available: 'Don't enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no man living is righteous' — the verse Paul echoes in Romans 3:20. A spirit overwhelmed, a soul that 'thirsts for you, like a parched land,' and the morning prayer: 'Cause me to hear your loving kindness in the morning… Teach me to do your will.' C19's door, and C09's thirst.

entries.pericope: His greatness is unsearchable… His tender mercies are over all his works
entries.connection: An acrostic of praise 'every day.' 'His greatness is unsearchable' is C24's; 'Yahweh is good to all. His tender mercies are over all his works… Yahweh upholds all who fall, and raises up all those who are bowed down… near to all those who call on him in truth' is C27's mercy with no one left outside it.

entries.pericope: Don't put your trust in princes… He upholds the fatherless and widow
entries.connection: 'Don't put your trust in princes… His spirit departs, and he returns to the earth. In that very day, his thoughts perish.' C18's release from trust in power. And the God who is trustworthy is identified by those he serves: the oppressed, the hungry, the prisoners, the blind, those bowed down, 'the foreigners… the fatherless and widow.' C16's list, in God's own character.

entries.pericope: He heals the broken in heart… He counts the number of the stars
entries.connection: Two kinds of greatness side by side: 'He heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds. He counts the number of the stars. He calls them all by their names.' The God of the galaxies attending to a wound — C19's healing and C24's wonder in one breath. 'He doesn't delight in the strength of the horse.'

entries.pericope: Praise him, sun and moon! Praise him, all you shining stars!
entries.connection: Everything summoned to praise in order — angels, sun and moon, sea creatures, hail and snow, fruit trees and cedars, wild animals, kings, young men and maidens, old men and children. C24's landscape, made a choir.

entries.pericope: Let everything that has breath praise Yah!
entries.connection: The Psalter ends in praise without argument and without petition: trumpet, harp, tambourine, dance, cymbals, 'Let everything that has breath praise Yah!' The book that has carried every lament to God ends where C10 says the road is going — delight.
